blocks.text: Sulfur combines with many elements to form a wide variety of inorganic and organic compounds. It is unreactive to water under normal conditions, to dilute non-oxidising acids and to the noble gases, and its ability to catenate lets it form ring structures and linear chains.

items: Sulfur burns in air to SO2 with a blue flame; the other main oxide SO3 needs a higher temperature and a catalyst: S + O2 gives SO2; 2SO2 + O2 over Pt gives 2SO3. Nitric acid oxidises sulfur to NO2 and sulfuric acid: S + 6HNO3 gives H2SO4 + 6NO2 + 2H2O.

With elements of lower electronegativity sulfur acts as an oxidising agent and forms sulfides; it tarnishes Ag, Cu and Zn with a coating of metal sulfide (2Ag + S gives Ag2S; Hg + S gives HgS; 2Cu + S gives Cu2S) but does not react with Au or Pt.
Sulfur converts cyanide into thiocyanate, a pseudohalide used to analyse Fe3+: KCN + S gives KSCN.

Sulfur reacts directly with fluorine to give SF4 and SF6; sulfur hexafluoride is a very unreactive gas used as an insulator in electrical devices (S + 3F2 gives SF6). It readily reacts with chlorine to give S2Cl2 (yellow liquid), which reacts further to SCl2 (red liquid): 2S + Cl2 gives S2Cl2.

blocks.prompt: How does sulfur react with halogens, and with HCl and NaOH (exercise Q.2i; Quick Check 12.5b)?
blocks.explanation: With fluorine it burns to SF4 and SF6, the hexafluoride being an inert insulating gas; with chlorine it gives yellow S2Cl2 and then red SCl2. Sulfur does not react with dilute non-oxidising HCl. With hot concentrated NaOH it disproportionates to sulfide and thiosulfate: 4S + 6NaOH gives 2Na2S + Na2S2O3 + 3H2O.

items: S burns to SO2 (SO3 needs Pt and heat); HNO3 gives H2SO4 + NO2; forms sulfides with Ag, Cu, Zn, Hg (not Au, Pt); KCN to KSCN; F2 to SF6 (inert), Cl2 to S2Cl2 and SCl2; inert to water, dilute acids, noble gases.
